prose_changes.old: Reform child of Cluny; shapes later mysticism
prose_changes.new: A plainer reform of Benedictine life, begun at Cîteaux in 1098. Bernard's writings fed later Western prayer.
prose_changes.reason: 'Reform child of Cluny' misstates the founding: the entry's own description has the founders leave Molesme, not Cluny, and no vendored text ties the Cistercians to Cluny at all (Bernard's Apologia and the Exordium Parvum are not vendored; listed in wants). 'Shapes later mysticism' is kept in plainer words and now carried by the documented link to the English mystics. Whole field rewritten.

prose_changes.old: In 1098 a group of monks walked out of the great Burgundian abbey of Molesme because they thought Benedictine life had grown too comfortable — Cluny and the other rich houses above all. And settled in a marshy clearing called Cîteaux to keep the Rule of St Benedict as plainly as they could: bare churches, simple food, no elaborate liturgy, and their own hands in the fields. Within a generation the reform had a constitution, the Carta Caritatis, binding every daughter house to the mother house through annual visitation and a yearly general chapter, and after Bernard of Clairvaux arrived in 1113 the order spread across Europe at extraordinary speed. Much of the actual labor was done by lay brothers, the conversi, who took vows but lived a separate, largely manual life alongside the choir monks on farms called granges. The order never ended, and its writers — Bernard on the Song of Songs, Aelred of Rievaulx on friendship — stayed among the most-read spiritual authors of the Latin West for centuries afterward.

prose_changes.old: The order is still here: Cistercian and Trappist houses keep the same rule today. Its buildings became a style of their own — the bare, unpainted, superbly proportioned church that architects still simply call Cistercian, of which Fontenay in Burgundy survives almost complete. Its writers stayed in circulation for centuries. Bernard's sermons on the Song of Songs and Aelred's Spiritual Friendship shaped nearly every later Western tradition of contemplative prayer and warm, affectionate devotion. And the granges left a mark on European farming, water management and land clearance that outlasted the monks who worked them.
prose_changes.new: The order is still here. Cistercian and Trappist houses keep the same rule today. Its buildings became a style of their own: the bare, unpainted, finely shaped church that architects still simply call Cistercian. Fontenay in Burgundy survives almost whole. Its writers were read for centuries. Bernard's sermons on the Song of Songs and Aelred's Spiritual Friendship fed a warm, loving strand of Western prayer. Two hundred years on, the English writers Richard Rolle and Walter Hilton still quoted Bernard by name. And the granges left a mark on European farming, on water and on the clearing of land that outlasted the monks who worked them.

Paragraph rewritten for reading level; the Trappist, Fontenay and granges facts kept.

prose_changes.old: The desert revived inside the Latin West
prose_changes.new: A hermit life of cell and silence in the Latin West, kept in much the same shape since 1084

prose_changes.old: The order is still living and still small, which is exactly what it intended. Its longest reach is Guigo II's Ladder of Monks: the four-step pattern of reading, meditating, praying and resting in God passed into the general devotional vocabulary of the West and is still taught today, often by people who have never heard of the Carthusians. The charterhouse plan — a great cloister ringed by individual cells and gardens — became a recognizable building type across Europe, and several former charterhouses now serve as museums and galleries. The liqueur the monks of the Grande Chartreuse still make has kept the name in ordinary circulation long after most people forgot what it belonged to.

Its four steps of reading, meditating, praying and resting in God were put into English in the fourteenth century. The author of The Cloud of Unknowing seems to have known them. The pattern is still taught today, often by people who have never heard of the Carthusians. The charterhouse plan, a great cloister ringed by single cells and gardens, became a familiar building type across Europe. Several former charterhouses now serve as museums and galleries. The monks of the Grande Chartreuse still make a liqueur, which keeps the name in everyday use long after most people forgot what it belonged to.

'Still taught today' kept. Paragraph rewritten for reading level; charterhouse and liqueur facts kept.

prose_changes.old: The abbey is gone, but the way of life is not: canons regular still exist, and Norbert's Premonstratensians remain an order today. The Victorines' real bequest was intellectual. Hugh's insistence that the arts and sciences belong inside the search for God, and Richard's stage-by-stage analysis of contemplation, were read and quarried by nearly everyone who wrote on prayer in the later Middle Ages — Bonaventure most of all. And the abbey's sequences stayed in the liturgy long after the school that composed them had gone quiet.

prose_changes.old: Mount Athos never stopped. Its monasteries have been continuously occupied since this period, still governed by their own charters, and it is one of the very few places on the whole map of Christian history where a visitor can find something doing today what it was doing a thousand years ago. The prayer practices formed here fed directly into hesychasm and the Palamite theology of the next century, and from there into the whole later devotional life of Orthodoxy — the Jesus Prayer, and eventually the Philokalia. Athonite typika were adapted by Georgian, Serbian, Bulgarian and Russian founders, exporting a model of monastic government across Eastern Europe.
prose_changes.new: Mount Athos never stopped. Its monasteries have been lived in without a break since this period, and their own charters still govern them. It is one of very few places on the whole map of Christian history where a visitor can find something doing today what it did a thousand years ago. The ways of prayer formed here fed straight into hesychasm and the Palamite theology of the next century. From there they passed into the whole later prayer life of Orthodoxy: the Jesus Prayer, and in time the Philokalia. Monks formed on Athos also carried its life outward. Anthony, who began the Caves Monastery at Kyiv, had taken his vows on the Holy Mountain. At Iviron, the Georgian house on Athos, monks put scripture and Greek books of theology into Georgian.
